body:
## Begin with something you want to understand

A large Buddhist library becomes welcoming when you enter with a small question. What does wisdom mean in the Heart Sutra? Why does the Lotus Sutra teach through stories? How can a rule about shared possessions illuminate life in a monastery? You can begin wherever your curiosity is strongest. A few sentences read attentively will give you a firmer footing than a long list of unfamiliar titles.

This guide introduces the Chinese Buddhist canon and offers a first route through Taixu Hall. The library brings scriptures, commentaries, and teachers into conversation. If Buddhist literature is new to you, start with one short scripture and keep a notebook beside you. Write down who is speaking, what the passage asks its listeners to understand, and one phrase you would like to revisit. These simple questions remain useful throughout a lifetime of study.

## What “Chinese Buddhist canon” means

Here, “Chinese” names the principal language in which the collection was transmitted. Its books preserve the work of translators from across Asia as well as generations of East Asian authors. Indian teachings acquired Chinese expressions; Chinese readers wrote commentaries and developed new ways to teach them. The collection thus offers both Buddhist teachings and a record of people learning to communicate them across languages.

The traditional name *Tripiṭaka* means “three baskets”: sutras, monastic discipline, and systematic analysis. A sutra commonly presents a teaching in a setting with named speakers and listeners. Vinaya literature explains the rules and procedures of the monastic community. Abhidharma examines experience through carefully arranged categories. Chinese canonical collections also include treatises, commentaries, biographies, catalogues, and historical writing. Each kind of book invites a slightly different reading pace.

For an English reading companion, the [BDK English Tripiṭaka project](https://www.bdkamerica.org/the-translation-project/) publishes translations of works from the Chinese canon. Its books can help you follow an argument while becoming familiar with the Chinese title and the text's place in the larger collection. On this site, the English catalogue provides an entrance to the library; check each work's page for the languages available in its actual text.

## Learn one useful address system

The Taishō canon was published in Japan between 1924 and 1934. Its reference numbers are widely used in Buddhist studies. T251, for example, identifies the Heart Sutra associated with Xuanzang; T262 identifies the Lotus Sutra associated with Kumārajīva. A fuller reference adds the volume, page, column, and line. Keeping the work number in your notes makes it much easier to find the same text in another catalogue.

The Taishō shelves group related materials: Āgama scriptures, Perfection of Wisdom texts, Lotus and Flower Garland scriptures, esoteric texts, Vinaya, and treatises, followed by commentaries and historical collections. [CBETA's catalogue explanation](https://archive2.cbeta.org/cbreader/help/cbeta_toc_en.htm) shows both this arrangement and its digital regrouping of related scriptures and commentaries. A digital library can bring a root text and its later interpreters together even when they occupy different printed volumes.

Use **By canon** on this site when you want to explore those bibliographical families. Use a teacher's page when you want to follow a person's writings and intellectual relationships. These two routes complement each other: one places a book among related texts, while the other places it among the people who studied and transmitted it.

## Meet two translators

[Kumārajīva](/en/masters/kumarajiva) worked in Chang'an, today's Xi'an, in the early fifth century. His translations include the Lotus Sutra and the Middle Treatise. Opening those two works side by side reveals the range of a translator's task: one unfolds through assemblies, parables, and verse; the other proceeds through tightly argued questions and answers. Both became lasting resources for Chinese Buddhist learning.

[Xuanzang](/en/masters/xuanzang), active in the seventh century, travelled to India and returned to China with Buddhist texts. His translation work is especially important for Yogācāra, the tradition concerned with cognition and its transformation. His name also appears in the heading of the familiar Chinese Heart Sutra. When you encounter a translator's name, pause over it: it connects the page before you to a particular history of travel, language, and study.

## Choose a first text

For a short beginning, read the [Heart Sutra](/en/classics/般若波羅蜜多心經), T251. Locate the opening in which Avalokiteśvara contemplates the five aggregates, then follow the address to Śāriputra. Notice how the text moves from form and emptiness through lists of Buddhist teachings to freedom from fear and its closing mantra. Read the whole scripture once before trying to resolve every unfamiliar term. On a second reading, concentrate on just one passage.

For a narrative beginning, choose chapter 3 of the [Lotus Sutra](/en/classics/妙法蓮華經), T262. Its burning-house parable presents a father seeking to bring his children to safety. Follow the story's sequence, then consider how the scripture uses it to explain the Buddha's teaching. Chapter 2 introduces skillful means and the one vehicle; chapter 5 returns to diversity through the image of rain nourishing different plants. These three chapters make a rewarding first group.

For a devotional beginning, read the [Amitābha Sutra](/en/classics/阿彌陀經), T366. Begin with its description of Sukhāvatī, Amitābha's land, and then find the passages on hearing and holding the Buddha's name. Ask how the landscape, the community, and the reader's aspiration belong together. This is a manageable introduction to the language of Pure Land Buddhism.

## Let commentary deepen the reading

A commentary gives you the company of another reader. It may explain a word, divide an argument into stages, connect one scripture with another, or show how a teaching enters practice. Begin by finding the exact sentence under discussion. Read the sentence, then its explanation, then the sentence again. This movement between text and commentary often makes a difficult paragraph much more approachable.

The eight schools provide another helpful map: Sanlun, Consciousness-Only, Tiantai, Huayan, Chan, Pure Land, Vinaya, and Esoteric Buddhism. Their interests range from reasoning and contemplation to devotion, community, and ritual. [Taixu](/en/masters/taixu), who lived from 1890 to 1947, valued all eight. In his account of his own intellectual development, he described their shared aim of buddhahood alongside their distinctive approaches to practice. That generous breadth informs the library named after him.

For your first week, return to the same short passage on three occasions. First follow its sequence; next explore one important term; finally consult a commentary or a teacher's page. Record the title, work number, and passage each time. Gradually your notebook will become a map of questions that matter to you, with a dependable path back to the sources.

## Where to go next

- [Read the Heart Sutra](/en/classics/般若波羅蜜多心經), beginning with Avalokiteśvara's contemplation of the five aggregates.
- [Open the Lotus Sutra](/en/classics/妙法蓮華經) and read the burning-house parable in chapter 3.
- [Explore the eight schools](/en/start/eight-schools) through their teachers and characteristic texts.
- [Meet Xuanzang](/en/masters/xuanzang) and follow his connections with translated scriptures and treatises.
- [Meet Taixu](/en/masters/taixu), whose broad approach to Buddhist learning shapes this library.
description: Find your first Buddhist text, learn how the Chinese canon is arranged, and build a reading practice with sutras, teachers, and commentaries.
kicker: A library, a history, a place to begin

master_cards.description_en: Kumārajīva (344–413) grew up in Kucha and studied Buddhist teachings in Central Asia and Kashmir.
Xuanzang (602–664) travelled through Central Asia to India to resolve questions about Buddhist doctrine.
Taixu advocated reforms of Buddhist institutions, monastic education and religious practice in modern China.

title: Start Here: Reading the Chinese Buddhist Canon

The Dharmaguptaka collection of monastic rules and accounts of their establishment.
A Chan collection of teachings attributed to Huineng, compiled in the name of Fahai.
